title: Adjusting Imports of Timber, Lumber, and Their Derivative Products Into the United States
summary:
The United States will impose new tariffs on a range of wood products to boost domestic production and address a national security concern tied to reliance on imports. Starting October 14, imports of softwood timber and lumber face a 10 percent tariff, while upholstered wood furniture and kitchen cabinets and vanities face a 25 percent tariff that rises on January 1, 2026 to 30 percent and 50 percent, respectively.

The policy is meant to help U.S. mills, manufacturers, and forest-product workers by encouraging investment, keeping plants open, and strengthening the supply of materials used in defense, energy, transport, and construction. Supporters argue it could create jobs, raise factory utilization, and make key supply chains more reliable, especially for items considered important to national security. There are also plans to monitor imports and, if needed, add more products or adjust how tariffs are applied to prevent underpricing.

However, the changes will likely raise costs for businesses that rely on imported wood inputs and finished goods—especially furniture makers, cabinet shops, homebuilders, and retailers. That could flow through to higher prices for new homes and renovations, and tighter margins for small and mid-sized firms that can’t quickly switch suppliers. Foreign suppliers and trading partners may also feel the impact, though imports from the United Kingdom will not face more than a 10 percent tariff, and imports from the European Union and Japan are capped so total rates do not exceed 15 percent. Ongoing talks with trading partners could lead to adjustments, and the government will review market conditions next year, including whether to consider hardwood products.

In short, this move aims to rebuild domestic capacity and reduce vulnerabilities. Its benefits will be most visible in U.S. wood production and related communities, while the near-term costs will likely be borne by import-reliant industries and consumers facing higher prices.
